blocks.text: As Draupadī was forcefully pulled by her hair into the sabhā, Duhśāsana attempted to disrobe her, but she was saved by Bhagavān Kṛṣṇa. Bhīma, overflowing with rage, vowed to kill Duhśāsana in war, to tear open his chest and drink his blood. Draupadī was further vilified by Karṇa and Duryodhana. Duryodhana taunted Draupadī by gesturing to her to come and sit on his thigh, indicating her servitude to him. Bhīma, infuriated, made a second Pratijñā that he would break Duryodhana's thigh in battle.
Like the other Pratijñā's we discussed so far, Bhīma too took these vows reacting to his emotions. However, these Pratijñās are markedly different - let us see how.

In Udyoga Parva, we see the Pāṇḍavas requesting their kingdom back from the Kauravas, as agreed in the 'Game of Dice'. Duryodhana however, refuses this request and all other requests made by the Pāṇḍavas. Though war seemed inevitable, Bhagavān Kṛṣṇa went as a peace messenger to the court of the Kauravas to negotiate a peaceful resolution to the conflict with Duryodhana. Kṛṣṇa consulted all the five Pāṇḍavas and Draupadī before his journey to meet Duryodhana. Surprisingly, Bhīma approved of peace rather than war, just like his elder brother Yudhiṣṭira. He was willing to forgo his Pratijñās to kill Duryodhana and Duhśāsana. Here we see that he did not ponder the question of war or peace in light of the Pratijñā he made.
